text: Common species affects the utility of non-invasive genetic monitoring of a cryptic endangered mammal: The bridled nailtail wallaby

Non-invasive methods of monitoring wild populations (such as genotyping faeces or hair) are now widely used and advocated. The potential advantages of such methods over traditional direct monitoring (such as live capture) are that accuracy improves because sampling of non-trappable individuals may be possible, species in difficult and remote terrain can be surveyed more efficiently, and disturbance to animals is minimal. Few studies have assessed the effects of interactions between species on remote sampling success.We test the use of non-invasive monitoring for the cryptic, forest-dwelling, solitary and endangered bridled nailtail wallaby (Onychogalea fraenata) that is sympatric with the ecologically similar and more common black-striped wallaby (Macropus dorsalis). Six types of hair traps were tested for 3668 trap days, and hairs were caught with about a 10% success rate. Camera traps showed that baited hair traps targeted both wallaby species. We microscopically identified hair as bridled nailtail wallaby or black-striped wallaby. We compared these hairs and their genotypes (using seven microsatellite loci) with known bridled nailtail wallaby hairs and genotypes derived from animal trapping. Trapped bridled nailtail wallaby hairs had characteristics that could be mistaken for black-stripe wallaby hairs; characteristics were not diagnostic. Genetic assignment tests consistently differentiated the known bridled nailtail wallaby samples from identified black-striped wallaby samples, however genetic overlap between most of the microsatellite markers means that they are not suitable for species identification of single samples, with the possible exception of the microsatellite locus B151. With similar trapping effort and within the same area, live-capture mark-recapture techniques estimated 40-60 individuals and non-invasive methods only detected 14 genotypes. A species-specific genetic marker would allow more efficient targeting of bridled nailtail wallaby samples and increase capture rates.

Quantifying the abundance and distribution of an endangered species is essential to successful management. Traditional methods may be inefficient and inaccurate if the species is cryptic. For instance, low capture rates are common in trap-shy animals (Hoyle et al. 1995) or large standard errors can obscure population size trends (Fisher et al. 2000). Non-invasive, remote detection methods are useful alternatives for many animals, as they negate the need to physically see or handle the animals. Remote methods involve recording signs such as footprints, photographs from camera traps (Kauffman et al. 2007;Treves et al. 2010), or analysing biological materials such as scats or hairs sampled by bait stations with sticky tape or hair snares (Reed 2011) or located using visual searches or by sniffer dogs (Long et al. 2007). Non-invasive methods have sometimes improved the precision of population estimations compared with traditional methods (Banks et al. 2003;Waits & Paetkau 2005;Bradley et al. 2008;Harris et al. 2010;Brook et al. 2012).
Successful non-invasive methods that permit estimates of population size and demography need to be appropriate for the species or population's ecology and behaviour (Améndola-Pimenta et al. 2009), and repeatable (Wilson & Delahay 2001;Waits & Paetkau 2005). Placement of hair traps is straightforward for mammals that repeatedly use the same areas and/or leave conspicuous evidence of their presence (such as at latrines, rub-sites or burrows), for example in population sampling of the northern hairy-nosed wombat (Lasiorhinus krefftii) (Sloane et al. 2000), the American pika (Ochotona princeps) (Henry & Russello 2011), and black bears (Ursus americanus) (Boersen et al. 2003). For mammals that do not use consistent trails, researchers have used attractants, such as for the European wildcats (Felis silvestris) (Kéry et al. 2011), fishers (Martes pennanti) and American martens (M. americana) (Williams et al. 2009). However, non-invasive monitoring is more difficult if the rare target species is sympatric with ecologically, behaviourally and morphologically similar common, non-target species which are also potentially attracted and sampled by the same methods, and may interact with the target species (Downey et al. 2007).
Here we examine the potential use of non-invasive monitoring of an endangered Australian macropod, the bridled nailtail wallaby.The bridled nailtail wallaby now occurs naturally in only one very small population in a conservation reserve (Taunton Scientific National Park) in central Queensland, Australia and population monitoring is central to its conservation management. There are also two translocated populations in central and western Queensland and a free-range fenced population in western New South Wales (Lundie-Jenkins & Lowry 2005). This species once occurred in a large area of the western slopes and adjacent plains of the Great Dividing Range in three states of eastern Australia (Fisher 2000). It declined severely in the late nineteenth century and was presumed extinct until its rediscovery in 1973. The bridled nailtail wallaby is a small (3-7 kg), solitary, forest-dwelling macropod with cryptic behaviour. The sympatric black-striped wallaby is a much more common species with similar ecology and overlapping body size (5-16 kg) (Evans 1996). At Taunton, blackstriped wallabies are widespread in all vegetation types, and attain densities up to six times as high as those of bridled nailtail wallabies (for unknown reasons, perhaps related to their larger size, more grass-based diet and more flighty temperament; Evans 1996; Dawson et al. 1992).
We tested the feasibility of remotely obtaining hairs from the endangered target species and distinguishing them from the non-target species. Morphological identification of hairs has been used in the past to distinguish the bridled nailtail wallaby from other species sheltering inside hollow logs such as rabbits and rufous bettongs (Aepyprymnus rufescens) (Fisher 2000). Black-striped wallabies do not use hollow logs (Evans 1996). Black-stripe wallaby and bridled nailtail wallaby scats are indistinguishable so this was not an option for non-invasive monitoring. Seven polymorphic microsatellite markers have also been successfully used for individual identification in past reproduction and translocation studies of the bridled nailtail wallaby (Sigg et al. 2005).These markers have never been used on the black-striped wallaby; therefore we assessed the genetic overlap of these markers for these two species to determine whether they can be used for non-invasive monitoring of bridled nailtail wallabies. We compared the number of individuals obtained from remote hair genotyping to population estimates from concurrent live-trapping of the bridled nailtail wallaby at Taunton.

The only wild population of the bridled nailtail wallaby occurs in Taunton Scientific National Park (149°11′E, 23°34′S), a reserve of 11 500 ha dedicated to this species in central Queensland (Gordon & Lawrie 1980). The mean annual rainfall of Taunton Scientific National Park is 711 mm; half of this falls between December and February. The National Park consists of two former cattle properties, one purchased by the Queensland government in 1979 and one in 1986. Major vegetation associations include woodland dominated by poplar box (Eucalyptus populnea), regrowth forest of brigalow (Acacia harpophylla) with yellowwood (Terminalia oblongata), woodland with dawson gum (Eucalyptus cambageana), rosewood (A. rhodoxylon), or lancewood (A. shirleyi), silver-leafed ironbark (E. melanophloia) with small-flowered bloodwood (E. polycarpa), or narrow-leafed ironbark (E. crebra). Nearly all of the wallaby population occurs in one section of brigalow regrowth vegetation which is about 5 km 2 in the north east section of the park. Nine cattle properties have common boundaries with the National Park, and most of the perimeter is cleared pasture.

We set 262 hair traps at Taunton Scientific National Park during one week in April and two weeks in June 2010 in the north-eastern section of the park, in areas where the population of bridled nailtail wallabies is most dense. Existing three-strand wire fences were incorporated into the sampling design, because hairs were evident on fences separating the reserve from the neighbouring property. We used doublesided heavy duty carpet tape (Blackwoods Pty Ltd, 'tape'). Our 6 hair trap designs were (i) 'high wire', tape on barbed strand 400 mm from ground level, set in gaps in the vegetation (n = 52); (ii) 'low wire', tape on plain strand 200 mm from ground level (n = 23); (iii) 'trap' (n = 94), tape strung across the entrance of locked-open traps (see below); (iv) 'trip-rope' (n = 29), vinyl clothes-line strung between trees in a triangle, with tape attached lengthwise along all of the rope, 200 mm from ground level; (v) 'single-rope' (n = 24) as in 4, but only one strand between two trees; and (vi) 'wafer' (n = 40), commercially available hair traps (Fauna Tech). These commercial traps are plastic half-cones pegged to the ground, with a sticky wafer lining inside the roof to collect the hairs, and a bait chamber at the narrow end containing lucerne pellets or sweet potato. On 633 trap-nights, 408 non-wafer hair traps were baited with a large handful of lucerne under the tape. All hair traps were checked 1-3 times over an average interval of 2.9 ± 0.1 (mean ± SE) days. If hairs were present, a section of tape was removed and stored on non-stick paper, along with a label recording the date and location. Removed sections of tape were replaced with fresh tape. We set camera traps (Reconyx RC55) at 7 hair trap sample locations in April and May for 2-8 nights at a time (n = 2 'high wire', n = 1 'trap', n = 2 'triprope', n = 2 'low wire'), and recorded the number of bridled nailtail wallabies and non-target species visiting each location per night. Our methods were approved by the University of Queensland Animal Ethics Committee (SBS/480/09) under Queensland Scientific Purposes Permit WITK06725610.
To compare population census of non-invasive sampling with current techniques and to provide hair samples of 'known' individuals we trapped bridled nailtail wallabies in June 2010 with park managers. We used 191 wire traps (380 × 380 × 760 mm) on four consecutive nights and recorded locations with a GPS. Cage traps were set in the same area as hair traps. Traps were baited with lucerne. We locked traps open to acclimatize the animals for two weeks before trapping. During trapping, each trap was checked two or three times a night. The animals were individually marked with a microchip (Trovan). We plucked hair samples from trapped wallabies, and stored them at room temperature on non-stick paper. Data from previous trapping sessions 2008-2009, using the same sampling method and intensity were obtained from park managers. These data were used to estimate the population size within the area sampled by hair trapping (see below).
We processed the hair samples in a pre-PCR room dedicated to handling samples with small amounts of DNA. DNA was extracted from samples 1-4 months after collection. Because it was not possible to be sure that multiple hairs on a tape were from the same animal, we took only one hair from each tape for DNA analysis. Each tape was checked under a dissecting microscope for putative bridled nailtail wallaby hairs. Hairs were only used if whole. We removed follicles under a dissecting microscope as close as possible to the base, and placed them into the bottom of a microcentrifuge tube for subsequent DNA extraction. We kept the remaining shaft in a zip-lock bag, with a corresponding number for subsequent identification.
We identified hair shafts to species using the published key for Australian mammals (Brunner & Triggs 2002) (see below). We examined cross-sectional characteristics when medulla patterns were ambiguous. We compared hairs with the species list of mammals found at Taunton National Park. Known bridled nailtail wallaby hairs were obtained from cage-trapped individuals and compared with hair trap samples.
We genetically analysed samples microscopically identified as bridled nailtail wallabies from hair traps ('nailtail-tape'), hair samples from cage-trapped bridled nailtail wallabies ('nailtail-cage') and hair samples microscopically identified as black-striped wallabies from hair traps ('blackstripetape'). We extracted DNA using a final volume of 20 μL reactions of Proteinase K (25 mg mL -1 ) in Hair Lysis Buffer (67 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.8, 16.6 mM (NH4)2SO4, 0.45% Triton X-100, 0.2 mg mL -1 Gelatin, 2.5 mM MgCl2, 0.25 μL Tween 20). Solutions were heated at 50°C for 45 min, immediately followed by 45 min at ≥85°C (Améndola-Pimenta et al. 2009). Tubes were centrifuged at 13 000 rpm for 30 s, before and after heating.
We used seven polymorphic microsatellite loci to obtain genotypes (Y105, B29, B87, B90, B123, B151 and Ym148; Pope et al. 1996;Sigg et al. 2005). We first screened samples with the B90 marker (a marker that tended to produce the strongest results) and only samples that amplified were analysed further. PCR reactions had a final volume of 10 μL and contained 2 μL of DNA template, 0.17 μM of each primer and 2 μL of 2 × Qiagen Multiplex PCR Master Mix (3 mM MgCl2). The remaining 6 loci were amplified in a multiplex. Amplifications were carried out with an initial denaturation at 94°C for 15 min, then 40 cycles of 94°C for 30 s, 58°C for 90 s, 72°C for 90 s, with a final cycle at 94°C for 30 s, 55°C for 60 s and 72°C for 60 s. The products were separated by capillary electrophoresis on an ABI 3130xl Genetic Analyzer. Bridled nailtail wallaby samples amplifying less than four loci on the first attempt were discarded and all loci for the remaining samples were amplified twice.We accepted a genotype at a given locus if it was observed on both amplifications and treated inconsistent genotypes as missing data.

We used a Weibull survival model to compare the success of each hair trap design in obtaining hairs, and to test the effect of baiting versus not baiting hair traps, in R (R Development Core Team 2012). Each day of sampling was considered independent; therefore, some of the same trap locations are represented on multiple dates. We tested if the number of wallabies of each species that visited hair traps of each design as detected by the camera traps differed using a t-test.
Matching genotypes were screened and deleted (at least 6/7 matching loci) and allele frequencies obtained using Microsatellite Toolkit v3.1.1 (Park 2001). Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium and the probability of identity between individuals (PI; the probability that at least two individuals in the population would have the same genotype for the loci examined; Mills et al. 2000) and between siblings (PIsib; Waits et al. 2001) were estimated in GenAlEx 6.4 (Peakall & Smouse 2006). The mean allelic dropout per locus was calculated following Pompanon et al. (2005).
To determine if blackstripe-tape samples could be genetically discerned from nailtail-tape samples, we used the program STRUCTURE v2.3.3 (Pritchard et al. 2000) to group the samples into clusters with no a priori information about species identification. This analysis assumes clusters have a given set of allele frequencies based on Hardy-Weinberg and linkage equilibrium and probabilistically assigns samples to a simulated number of K clusters over a set of Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) iterations (Pritchard et al. 2000) after discarding a set of burn in iterations. For each K (1-5) we performed 20 independent runs with 100 000 MCMC iterations, assuming a model of admixture and independent allele frequencies. We inferred the number of K using the maximum likelihood and the ΔK method (Evanno et al. 2005). We also undertook assignment tests in which nailtail-tape samples were probabilistically assigned to pre-determined reference 'populations' of nailtail-cage or blackstripe-tape in GeneClass2 based on Bayesian algorithms (Rannala & Mountain 1997;Piry et al. 2004) and in GenAlEx 6.4 based on allele frequencies (Peakall & Smouse 2006). Genetic differentiation (Fst) between the resulting STRUCTURE clusters was calculated using FreeNA (Chapuis & Estoup 2007).
According to the key (Brunner & Triggs 2002), bridled nailtail wallaby hairs have a medulla with a uniserial ladder (regularly spaced and sized lighter patches) near the base of the hair and an oblong cross-section. Black-striped wallaby hairs have a simple medulla (no pattern) that can have vacuoles (that are displayed as lighter patches within the medulla that are of irregular length and width) and oval cross-section (Brunner & Triggs 2002). However, even known bridled nailtail wallaby hairs contained characters that could be mistaken for black-stripe wallaby hairs. For a majority of hairs we found that within a single hair, regular sized and spaced patterning in the medulla often preceded uneven patterning. We made tentative species identifications based on the length and spacing of these patterns; hairs were identified as bridled nailtail wallaby if the uniserial ladder was persistent on the majority of the length of the hair shaft, even if it became uneven. As we wished to encapsulate the variation and overlap of these characteristics, which was not displayed in the hair ID program, we assigned hairs into three groups based on consistently observed features. Our groupings were based on the progression of the medulla pattern from the base to the tip of the hair; 'uni-simple', 'uni-unevensimple' and 'uneven-simple'.The 'uni' pattern, as in uniserial ladder, had regularly spaced and sized lighter patches in the medulla. The medulla pattern was categorized as 'uneven' if the lighter patches were of irregular length and width. A simple medulla has no obvious structure. We compared the morphological and genetic species identification techniques. We used one-sided student t-tests to test if there were differences in mean length of hairs identified morphologically as bridled nailtail wallabies or black-striped wallabies, and between assigned clusters from the STRUCTURE analysis.
In order to compare the population estimate of bridled nailtail wallabies based on trapping with the hair sampling, we used trapping data only from the area sampled by the 144 hair traps from which samples were taken for DNA extraction. There were four capture occasions per session in June 2010, November 2009, May 2009, November 2008 and May 2008. We used MARK (White & Burnham 1999) to estimate population size with Huggins closed-population models (Huggins 1989). We fitted six candidate models; (i) sex and time dependence in the probability of capture (p), this was the most general model as it was the most parameterized; (ii) time dependence in p; (iii) sex dependence in p and in the probability of recapture (c) (differential p and c is interpreted as a behavioural response to trapping) (Otis et al. 1978); (iv) sex dependence in p; (v) behavioural response to trapping; and, (vi) all parameters constant. The sex covariate was eliminated for the trapping session May 2008, as there was only one female recapture. Model 1 was used to generate an estimate for the data dispersion parameter c ˆ(c-hat) (Lebreton et al. 1992), using the median c âpproach in MARK and, where appropriate, we used these values to adjust the Akaike information criterion for small sample sizes (QAICc) (Anderson et al. 1994). We compared the fit of the six candidate models based on the lowest QAICc or AICc value. Population size and values for p and c were derived using the model averaging approach in MARK.

section: success and species visitation rates of hair traps
text:
Two-hundred and sixty-two hair traps were sampled on 14 occasions (i.e. there were 3668 trap days in April and June). Hair was sampled on 372 trap days (about a 10% success rate). The most successful type of hair trap was the tape across the opening of locked-open cage traps during pre-feeding ('trap'). This design gained hairs more quickly (P < 0.001) than any other (with bait, estimated mean ± SE number of days to gain hair was 2.3 ± 0.2 days). On average, 56 ± 3% (n = 92) of the length of tapes from 'trap' design were covered in hair. Hair-traps attached to low wire fences ('low wire') and rope between trees ('trip-rope') were the next quickest to gain hairs (mean ± SE 5.1 ± 2.6 and 6.2 ± 0.3 days, respectively). The presence of lucerne bait significantly reduced the time before hair traps gained hair (P < 0.001; Fig. 1) for all hair trap types.
Camera traps were deployed on 30 trap-nights. We recorded 97 visits by bridled nailtail wallabies that appeared to make contact with a hair trap (3.2 ± 0.8 visits per hair trap per night) and 87 visits by blackstriped wallabies (2.9 ± 0.8). There was no significant difference in the number of visits to hair traps by bridled nailtail wallabies and black-striped wallabies (t 58 = -0.3, P = 0.76). There was a difference in the number of wallabies visiting different types of hair traps, consistent with hair sampling frequencies (above); 'trap' (7.8 ± 2.2 visits per hair trap per night) and 'trip-rope' designs (3.5 ± 0.8 visits per hair trap per night) received more visits from wallabies than low wire fences (2.2 ± 1.6), high wire fences (1.4 ± 0.6), or a single rope between two trees (1.5 ± 1.2) (overall model F9,50 = 2.3, P = 0.03). Different hair trap designs did not attract different species of wallabies: there was no significant interaction between trap design and wallaby species ('wafer' hair traps had no cameras).

We collected 149 hairs from 144 hair traps over five days. Initially, 90 hairs were microscopically identified as bridled nailtail wallabies (nailtail-tape), 38 as black-striped wallabies (blackstripe-tape), and 21 as other species. Sixty-seven individual hairs from different cage-trapped bridled nailtail wallaby individuals (nailtail-cage) were amplified. Forty-four percent of nailtail-tape samples (n = 40), 47% of blackstripe-tape (n = 18) and 54% of nailtail-cage samples (n = 36) samples amplified with four or more loci and were used in the analysis.
There were two matching genotypes between samples at 6/7 loci; one between a nailtail-tape and a nailtail-cage sample, another between two nailtail-cage samples. The probability that these samples were from different individuals and matched by chance (PI) was 1.06 × 10 -8 , or 1.78 × 10 -3 if they were siblings (PI-sib). These probabilities were small, relative to the estimated population size (about 100, A. Dinwoodie, pers. comm., QPWS, 2010) and consequently, we assumed that identical genotypes were from the same individual. One genotype from each of the matches was deleted in subsequent analyses. Interestingly, the two matching nailtail-cage samples had different pit tag numbers, highlighting that no marking technique is perfect. The mean allelic dropout per locus was between 0.05 and 0.19 (Table 1).

Genetic clustering analyses showed that nailtail-tape samples (morphologically identified hairs) consisted of both bridled nailtail wallaby and black-striped wallaby hairs (Table 2). In the program STRUC-TURE, the maximum absolute likelihood value was for K = 2 clusters. For K = 2, there was little admixture (all genotypes were assigned to a cluster with >0.9 likelihood). All nailtail-cage genotypes were clustered together (thereafter, cluster 1), all except one blackstripe-tape genotype were clustered separately (thereafter cluster 2), and nailtail-tape genotypes were clustered with either nailtail-cage or blackstripe-tape samples. The ΔK distribution peaked at K = 3, however, the same samples remained as differentiated as in K = 2; the additional clustering differentiated within genotype mixture (across genotypes within cluster 1) and provided no further information to differentiate samples. Assignment tests (both Bayesian and allele frequency methods) agreed with the results from the STRUCTURE analysis; the same nailtailtape genotypes that were grouped with either cluster 1 (n = 14) or 2 (n = 26) in STRUCTURE were assigned to reference populations nailtail-cage and blackstripetape, respectively. Fst was 0.267 (95% CI: 0.160, 0.395) between cluster 1 and cluster 2. We conclude that samples in cluster 1 were putatively bridled nailtail wallaby and samples in cluster 2 were putatively black-stripe wallaby and the discrepancy for the assignment of nailtail-tape samples was due to  misidentification (see below). The nailtail-tape samples assigned to cluster 1 were found on hair trap types 'trap' (n = 4), 'single-rope' (n = 1), 'low wire' (n = 6) and 'trip-rope' (n = 3). Most loci (5/7, except B90 and B87) were not in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium in hair samples identified morphologically as nailtail-tape. However, cluster analysis revealed that this group consisted of two species. After regrouping the samples into the two STRUCTURE clusters, three loci still significantly deviated from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium for cluster 1 and 2 and most of these loci had high proportions of allelic drop-out (Tables 1,3). Both cluster 1 and cluster 2 possessed private alleles and allelic overlap (Tables 1,3). B151 was the only locus that did not have genetic overlap between putatively identified species (Table 1) and the size range of the alleles was different for the two clusters; cluster 1201-243 bp and cluster 2196 bp.
According to the key (Brunner & Triggs 2002), bridled nailtail wallaby hairs have a uniserial ladder medulla pattern near the base and an oblong crosssection and black-striped wallaby hairs are simple but can have uneven vacuoles and an oval cross-section. However, rather than a dichotomy of features, hairs collected while trapping (nailtail-cage) also contained Note that the original morphological species identification was based on the length and spacing of the uniserial ladder, not presence alone. Cluster 1 contains putatively bridled nailtail wallaby samples; all trapped bridled nailtail wallabies samples (nailtail-cage), 14 bridled nailtail wallaby identified hair samples (nailtail-tape) and 1 black-striped wallaby identified sample (blackstripe-tape) from hair traps. Cluster 2 contains putatively black-stripe wallaby samples; 17 blackstripe-tape samples and 26 nailtail-tape samples. See methods text for medulla description definition. Cluster 1 contains putatively bridled nailtail wallaby samples; all trapped bridled nailtail wallabies samples (nailtail-cage), 14 bridled nailtail wallaby identified hair samples (nailtail-tape) and 1 black-striped wallaby identified sample (blackstripe-tape) from hair traps. Cluster 2 contains putatively black-stripe wallaby samples; 17 blackstripe-tape samples and 26 nailtail-tape samples.
uneven patterning which could have been mistaken for vacuoles of black-stripe wallaby hairs. Unsurprisingly, genetic analysis was inconsistent with morphological identification of single hairs as bridled nailtail wallaby or black-striped wallaby. The uniserial ladder would often become 'uneven' along the hair shaft. We assigned hairs that had a 'uni' medulla along the majority of the hair as bridled nailtail wallaby hairs, yet this feature did not consistently distinguish genetically similar samples (Table 2). Even only considering samples with a 'uni-simple' medulla (putatively a bridled nailtail wallaby characteristic), samples were assigned to both cluster 1 (n = 8) and cluster 2 (n = 5; Table 2). The vacuoles in the medulla of any putative black-striped wallaby hair appeared too similar to the uniserial ladder pattern of a putative bridled nailtail wallaby hair. Mean hair length was not significantly different between morphologically identified hairs (t 35 = -0.55, P > 0.29). Mean hair length was longer for samples in cluster 2 (putatively black-stripe wallaby) than cluster 1 (t16 = 2.93, P < 0.05). Nevertheless, the variation in hair lengths overlapped between the clusters and so this is not a reliable characteristic. Bridled nailtail wallaby, black-stripe wallaby and rufous bettong hairs all are dark with a light colour band in the straight shield region. All samples with an 'oblong' cross-section, a diagnostic feature of the bridled nailtail wallaby in the key (Brunner & Triggs 2002), were assigned to cluster 2 (putatively black-stripe wallaby; Table 2).

Amongst the genetically identified bridled nailtail wallaby hairs (cluster 1, n = 14) there were no identical matches (i.e. individuals were not recaptured). Therefore, no population estimate based on hair samples was possible. Based on cage trapping, the mean population size of the hair-sampled area was 40-60 animals (Table 4). Time varying probability of capture models had consistently the lowest QAICs, except for the June 2010 trapping session, where the sex + behaviour and sex models had the lowest QAICc (combined weight of 98%). In the same area that the hair traps were set, between 31 and 52 individual bridled nailtail wallabies were captured in trapping sessions in May 2008 and July 2010 and the weighted recapture probability was never greater than 0.3.

Distinguishing the bridled nailtail wallaby from the sympatric black-striped wallaby using hair morphology and genotyping gave inconsistent results. Bridled nailtail wallabies have been identified from hairs at this site before (Fisher 2000), although that study sampled hairs inside hollow logs and artificial shelters designed to mimic fallen timber: microhabitats not expected to be used by black-striped wallabies. In a study of Australian mammals using a previous version of the same key that we used, Lobert et al. (2001) showed through blind tests that morphological identification of hairs could be inaccurate, particularly between closely related species. Studies of other groups of mammals including Tasmanian, Brazilian, and North American placentals and marsupials have found that species identification of hairs from closely related species can be inaccurate because these species often have subtle and overlapping features (Taylor 1985;Wallis 1993;Sessions et al. 2009;Vanstreels et al. 2010). This study highlights that variation of characters is important to include in a diagnostic key as morphologies are rarely dichotomous and there may be overlap between closely related species.
Authors of the hair identification key (Brunner & Triggs 2002) recommend that a clump of hair be used for species identification, and some studies suggest taking multiple hairs for DNA extraction to increase genetic yields (Castro-Arellano et al. 2008;Ruibal et al. 2010). However, we were restricted to identifying one hair at a time because tapes often sampled too many hairs to distinguish where individuals had made contact, even in a brief sampling period. Nevertheless, even if multiple hairs were taken, DNA mixing between species and individuals would become a problem because it could result in false genotypes (see below).
The microsatellite markers used in this study were originally employed in genetic analysis for individual identification rather than species identification, so their design for species identification was sub-optimal. Although there were some private alleles between species, the limited allelic overlap of most of these markers was sufficient to preclude their use as identifiers. The locus B151 was the only marker that did not have any allelic overlap between the putatively The sex covariate was eliminated for the trapping session May 2008, as there was only one female recapture. identified species and the difference in the size range of the alleles could indicate species specificity for this locus. Although, we recommend further sequencing of known black-stripe samples would need to be done in order to clarify the use of this marker as a speciesidentifier. Other researchers have successfully used mitochondrial DNA markers taken from hair samples to distinguish species of North American carnivores and European small mammals (Moran et al. 2008;Clevenger & Sawaya 2010), and mitochondrial DNA can distinguish macropod species (Phillips et al. 2013). We suggest further testing of the B151 marker or the use of mitochondrial markers to improve the efficiency of laboratory procedures. Ensuring accurate species identification is important prior to microsatellite genotyping (which can identify individuals for capture-recapture models of population size).
Images from camera traps showed bridled nailtail wallabies visited the hair traps, and as predicted, the black-striped wallabies were also sampled. Fisher et al. (2000) found that although bridled nailtail wallabies are not territorial, they appear to follow consistent daily routines: radio-tracked animals consistently used the same shelter locations, and marked individuals were often seen at the same locations at the same times of day. We detected only a fraction of the number of individuals caught by cage traps. This suggests that a much greater sampling density would be needed to monitor an adequate proportion of the known population using remote hair sampling methods, assuming that all of the population is attracted to bait and/or uses sampled areas. An assumed advantage of remote sampling is the possibility of detecting the unknown proportion of untrappable or unseen individuals in a population of cryptic species (e.g. Andanje et al. 2011;Brook et al. 2012). Our results show that the most efficient collection of hairs on sticky tape was by placing tape in baited traps, indicating that remote hair trapping predominantly sampled the cage-trappable population of our study species. We show that hair sampling on rope strung between trees and on low wires is effective, especially if hair traps are baited, and a previous study at Taunton found that hair sampling inside potential shelters such as hollow logs can sample bridled nailtail wallabies without the problem of black-striped wallaby by-catch. A combination of hair trapping inside potential shelters, and a higher sampling effort on low wires throughout areas of potential habitat would improve the chance of sampling untrapped individual bridled nailtail wallabies. Fisher et al. (2000) found that traditional cagetrapping methods to estimate population trends of the bridled nailtail wallaby were problematic because of low and variable capture and recapture rates. They concluded that the trapping frequency would need to be unfeasibly high (i.e. too intrusive and potentially counterproductive) to detect changes in population size of a magnitude that would be useful to guide management responses to declines, such as supplementary feeding and additional predator control. Fisher et al. (2000) concluded that line-transect methods (distance sampling using spotlighting along forest tracks) gave more precise results. Distance sampling is much less intrusive and less labour intensive than trapping, and has been used successfully at Taunton to detect long-term population trends (Fisher et al. 2000). However, there has been a more than four-fold increase in the biomass of introduced buffel grass (Cenchrus ciliaris) at Taunton, including the north-east section inhabited by bridled nailtail wallabies, from 0.7 tonnes per hectare in the mid 1990s to more than 3 tonnes per hectare in 2009-2012(K. Donaldson, pers. comm. 2013)). This grass forms dense, tall stands which have substantially lowered visibility and made distance sampling less effective (Lundie-Jenkins & Lowry 2005).
Wang and Fisher (2012) used camera-trapping to estimate local distribution of bridled nailtail wallabies, which can be distinguished from other species by their markings in photographs. However, camera traps were unbaited and placed along roads in open areas to detect predators and bridled nailtail wallabies were only photographed during the dry season and at a low rate (1.4%). Camera trapping is not an option for population size estimation because natural markings do not consistently distinguish individuals for this species and a precision of individual identification is necessary (Foster & Harmsen 2012;Hamel et al. 2013). Even if individuals were trapped to apply unique tags for identification on camera traps (as was done with distance sampling method; Fisher et al. 2000), it would be too invasive and ineffective (not enough individuals sampled due to low capture rates and fast life history) to warrant the extra trapping effort.
Hair-trapping can successfully target bridled nailtail wallabies, but further work is needed using species specific markers to test whether this technique can be used to estimate population size at Taunton. Genetic data gained from trapped hairs could be used to assess genetic variation and drift, to identify where to trap individuals for relocation and captive breeding, and possibly to identify individuals not sampled with cagetrapping methods (using a larger sampling effort than in this study, including more sampling sites such as inside shelters).
Non-invasive methods for estimating population size and demography are increasingly advocated to complement or improve on traditional direct capturemark-recapture or resight methods, especially for conservation of solitary, medium to large forest mammals (Boulanger et al. 2008;Coster et al. 2011). The utility of this method is not universal, and may vary between populations. Some studies can take advantage of multi-species targeting (Long et al. 2007;Castro-Arellano et al. 2008;Williams et al. 2009), but as in some studies of carnivores (Downey et al. 2007;Long et al. 2007), we show that sympatric species can interfere with non-invasive sampling of macropods. Successful monitoring and management require tailored methods. This study highlights the need to carefully evaluate and verify techniques when applied to a new species.
